samples.title: Why we didn't rank your school
samples.body:
Every March, when the Department for Education publishes its attainment tables, we receive a handful of emails asking why the Ledger does not print a league table of Bristol's secondary schools. It is a fair question, and the honest answer is that we tried it once, in 2022, and regretted it.

The problem is not that the figures are wrong. It is that a single ranked list invites readers to treat a gap of one or two points as meaningful when, for schools with small year groups, it often is not. A school with ninety pupils sitting GCSEs can move ten places on the back of four or five results. Printing that movement as news would be accurate in the narrowest sense and misleading in every sense that matters.

So this year, as last year, we have published each school's figures alongside the city average and the range we would expect from chance alone. It makes for a less dramatic graphic. I think it makes for a more useful one, and I would rather defend that choice than a headline I could not stand behind.

samples.title: A note on our fly-tipping figures
samples.body:
A reader in Lockleaze wrote to point out that our map of fly-tipping reports appeared to show far more incidents on her street than she had ever seen. She was right to query it, though in this case the figures held up: the council logs each report, not each pile, so a single dumped sofa reported by six neighbours appears six times.

We should have said so more clearly in the original piece, and the explanatory note on the map has now been rewritten. The underlying point, that reports have risen by roughly a fifth since collection charges changed, stands.

samples.title: What 'up 9%' does and doesn't mean
samples.body:
Our story on Bristol rents drew a good deal of correspondence, most of it some version of 'my rent went up far more than that'. I do not doubt it. The 9% figure is the change in the median advertised rent for new lets, which is a different thing from what sitting tenants pay, and a very different thing from what any one household experiences.

I have added a short explainer to the article setting out where the number comes from and what it leaves out. If you think we have the picture wrong for your part of the city, I would genuinely like to hear from you; several of our better stories this year began as a reader telling us the data did not match their street.
